description: Wolfram Language carries physical units, dates and real-world entities as first-class computable objects rather than bare numbers. Quantity attaches units that propagate correctly through arithmetic and calculus, DateObject represents instants and granular dates with time zones and calendars, and the Entity framework gives access to the curated Wolfram Knowledgebase.

tools.name: Quantity
tools.description: Represents a physical quantity: a magnitude together with a unit, written Quantity[3, "Meters"]. Quantities participate in ordinary arithmetic with automatic unit checking and conversion, so adding incompatible units gives an error rather than a wrong number. Units may be compound expressions such as "Meters"/"Seconds" or named derived units such as "Newtons".
tools.example:
Quantity[3, "Meters"]
Quantity[3, "Meters"] + Quantity[50, "Centimeters"]
Quantity[100, "Kilometers"]/Quantity[2, "Hours"]
Quantity[1, "Mile"] > Quantity[1, "Kilometer"]
Quantity[9.8, "Meters"/"Seconds"^2]
tools.notes: Unit names are strings in the Wolfram unit ontology; Interpreter["Unit"]["mph"] or free-form input resolves informal names. Arithmetic between incompatible units returns unevaluated with a message.

tools.name: QuantityMagnitude
tools.description: Extracts the numeric magnitude from a Quantity, optionally converting to a specified unit first. QuantityMagnitude[q, unit] is the standard way to get a plain number in known units for further numeric work. Applied to a list of quantities it strips them all.
tools.example:
QuantityMagnitude[Quantity[3, "Meters"]]
QuantityMagnitude[Quantity[1, "Mile"], "Meters"]
QuantityMagnitude[Quantity[100, "Kilometers"/"Hours"], "Meters"/"Seconds"]
QuantityMagnitude[measurements, "Celsius"]
tools.notes: Always pass the target unit explicitly when stripping units for numerics, otherwise the magnitude may be in whatever unit the quantity happens to carry.

tools.name: QuantityUnit
tools.description: Gives the unit part of a Quantity as a unit expression, without the magnitude. It is used to inspect what units a computed result ended up in and to build a new quantity with the same units. The result can be passed straight back to Quantity or UnitConvert.
tools.example:
QuantityUnit[Quantity[3, "Meters"]]
QuantityUnit[Quantity[1, "Newtons"]]
QuantityUnit[Quantity[5, "Meters"]/Quantity[2, "Seconds"]]
Quantity[10, QuantityUnit[reference]]

tools.name: QuantityQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression is a valid Quantity with a recognized unit, returning True or False. Use it as an argument guard in functions that accept either plain numbers or quantities. KnownUnitQ tests a unit string on its own.
tools.example:
QuantityQ[Quantity[3, "Meters"]]
QuantityQ[3]
QuantityQ[Quantity[3, "Blorks"]]
KnownUnitQ["Furlongs"]
f[q_?QuantityQ] := QuantityMagnitude[q, "Meters"];

tools.name: UnitConvert
tools.description: Converts a quantity to a different but compatible unit, or to the corresponding SI base units when no target is given. It handles compound and derived units, temperature scales with offsets, and lists of quantities. Conversion between incompatible dimensions fails with a message.
tools.example:
UnitConvert[Quantity[1, "Mile"], "Kilometers"]
UnitConvert[Quantity[1, "Newtons"]]
UnitConvert[Quantity[98.6, "DegreesFahrenheit"], "DegreesCelsius"]
UnitConvert[Quantity[1, "Hours"], "Seconds"]
UnitConvert[{Quantity[1, "Feet"], Quantity[2, "Yards"]}, "Meters"]

tools.name: UnitSimplify
tools.description: Simplifies the units in an expression, cancelling matching units and combining them into the simplest equivalent form. It is what turns a messy product of units left by arithmetic into a recognizable derived unit such as Newtons or Watts. The magnitude is converted consistently.
tools.example:
UnitSimplify[Quantity[1, "Kilograms"] Quantity[1, "Meters"]/Quantity[1, "Seconds"]^2]
UnitSimplify[Quantity[3, "Meters"]/Quantity[1, "Meters"]]
UnitSimplify[Quantity[1, "Volts"] Quantity[1, "Amperes"]]
UnitSimplify[energy/time]

tools.name: CompatibleUnitQ
tools.description: Tests whether two or more quantities have units that can be converted into one another, i.e. share the same physical dimensions. Use it to validate input before arithmetic that would otherwise fail. It returns True for metres and miles, False for metres and seconds.
tools.example:
CompatibleUnitQ[Quantity[1, "Meters"], Quantity[1, "Feet"]]
CompatibleUnitQ[Quantity[1, "Meters"], Quantity[1, "Seconds"]]
CompatibleUnitQ[Quantity["Joules"], Quantity["NewtonMeters"]]
If[CompatibleUnitQ[a, b], a + b, $Failed]

tools.name: UnitDimensions
tools.description: Gives the physical dimensions of a unit or quantity as a list of {dimension, exponent} pairs, such as {{"LengthUnit", 1}, {"TimeUnit", -1}} for a speed. It is the basis of dimensional analysis and of checking that a formula is dimensionally consistent. CompatibleUnitQ is implemented by comparing these dimensions.
tools.example:
UnitDimensions["Newtons"]
UnitDimensions[Quantity[1, "Meters"/"Seconds"]]
UnitDimensions["Joules"] == UnitDimensions["NewtonMeters"]
UnitDimensions["Volts"]

tools.name: DateObject
tools.description: Represents a date or time with an explicit granularity (year, month, day, hour, minute, second or instant), calendar and time zone. Built from a date list, a string, or another date object, it supports comparison, arithmetic and formatting. It is the modern replacement for raw date lists and absolute times.
tools.usage:
DateObject[{y, m, d}]
DateObject[{y, m, d, h, min, s}]
DateObject["string"]
DateObject[date, "granularity", TimeZone -> tz]
tools.example:
DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}]
DateObject[{2024, 5, 17, 14, 30, 0}, TimeZone -> "America/New_York"]
DateObject["May 17 2024"]
DateObject[{2024}, "Year"]
DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}] + Quantity[30, "Days"]
tools.notes: Comparison and subtraction of DateObjects work directly and respect time zones; subtracting two of them gives a Quantity of time.

tools.name: DateString
tools.description: Formats a date as a string using named elements such as "Year", "MonthName", "Day", "Hour", "ISODateTime" or a full format list. With no argument it gives the current date and time. It is the standard way to produce timestamps for filenames, logs and reports.

parameters.name: elements
parameters.description: Format elements such as "Year", "Month", "Day", "Hour", "Minute", "Second", "MonthName", "DayName", or the presets "ISODate", "ISODateTime", "DateTime".

tools.example:
DateString[]
DateString["ISODate"]
DateString[{2024, 5, 17}, {"DayName", ", ", "MonthName", " ", "Day"}]
DateString[Now, {"Year", "Month", "Day", "Hour", "Minute"}]
"log_" <> DateString[{"Year", "Month", "Day"}] <> ".txt"

tools.name: DateValue
tools.description: Extracts named components from a date, such as "Year", "MonthName", "DayName", "ISOWeek", "Quarter" or "DayCount". Unlike DateString it returns computable values rather than formatted text. A list of element names returns several values at once.
tools.example:
DateValue[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}], "DayName"]
DateValue[Now, "Year"]
DateValue[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}], {"Year", "Month", "Day"}]
DateValue[Today, "ISOWeek"]
GroupBy[dates, DateValue[#, "Month"] &]

tools.name: DateList
tools.description: Converts a date to the plain list form {year, month, day, hour, minute, second}, which is the traditional numeric representation. It accepts date strings, absolute times and DateObjects, so it is also a parser. DateObject is the preferred modern representation, but DateList remains convenient for arithmetic on components.
tools.example:
DateList[]
DateList[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}]]
DateList["2024-05-17"]
DateList[3.8*^9]
First[DateList[Now]]

tools.name: AbsoluteTime
tools.description: Gives the number of seconds since the start of January 1, 1900, which is the Wolfram Language's absolute time origin. It is a single number, so it is convenient for sorting, differencing and storing timestamps compactly. FromAbsoluteTime and DateObject convert back to a readable date.
tools.example:
AbsoluteTime[]
AbsoluteTime[{2024, 5, 17}]
AbsoluteTime[Now] - AbsoluteTime[DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}]]
FromAbsoluteTime[3.9*^9]
SortBy[records, AbsoluteTime[#date] &]
tools.notes: The epoch is 1900, not 1970; use UnixTime and FromUnixTime when exchanging timestamps with other systems.

tools.name: DatePlus
tools.description: Adds a time increment to a date, with the increment given as a number of days or as {n, "unit"} for months, years, weeks, business days and so on. It handles calendar irregularities such as month lengths and leap years correctly. Adding a Quantity of time to a DateObject with ordinary + does the same thing for fixed-length units.
tools.example:
DatePlus[DateObject[{2024, 1, 31}], {1, "Month"}]
DatePlus[Today, 30]
DatePlus[Today, {2, "Week"}]
DatePlus[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}], {10, "BusinessDay"}]
DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}] + Quantity[3, "Days"]

tools.name: DateDifference
tools.description: Gives the amount of time between two dates as a Quantity, in days by default or in a requested unit such as "Year", "Month", "Hour" or "BusinessDay". A list of units returns a mixed representation, for example years plus months plus days. Simply subtracting two DateObjects gives the same information as a time Quantity.
tools.usage:
DateDifference[date1, date2]
DateDifference[date1, date2, "unit"]
DateDifference[date1, date2, {"u1", "u2"}]
tools.example:
DateDifference[DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}], DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}]]
DateDifference[{2024, 1, 1}, {2024, 5, 17}, "Week"]
DateDifference[birthdate, Today, "Year"]
DateDifference[start, end, "BusinessDay"]
Now - DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}]

tools.name: DayName
tools.description: Gives the day of the week of a date as a symbol such as Monday or Friday, with no argument giving today's. Related functions DayRange, DayCount and DayMatchQ work with business days, weekends and named day classes. These make calendar logic straightforward without manual modular arithmetic.
tools.usage:
DayName[]
DayName[date]
DayRange[d1, d2]
DayCount[d1, d2, "BusinessDay"]
DayMatchQ[date, class]
tools.example:
DayName[]
DayName[{2024, 5, 17}]
DayRange[DateObject[{2024, 5, 1}], DateObject[{2024, 5, 7}]]
DayCount[{2024, 1, 1}, {2024, 12, 31}, "BusinessDay"]
DayMatchQ[Today, Weekend]

tools.name: DateRange
tools.description: Generates a list of dates between two endpoints with a given increment, which may be a number of days or a {n, "unit"} specification. It is the date analogue of Range and is the natural way to build the time axis of a series. Day-class specifications such as "BusinessDay" skip weekends and holidays.
tools.usage:
DateRange[date1, date2]
DateRange[date1, date2, increment]
DateRange[date1, date2, "Month"]
tools.example:
DateRange[DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}], DateObject[{2024, 1, 7}]]
DateRange[{2024, 1, 1}, {2024, 12, 1}, "Month"]
DateRange[{2024, 1, 1}, {2024, 1, 31}, "BusinessDay"]
Length[DateRange[start, end, Quantity[1, "Weeks"]]]

tools.name: TimeObject
tools.description: Represents a time of day without a date, with an optional time zone and granularity. It supports comparison and arithmetic within a day and is what DateObject uses for its time component. Use it for schedules and recurring daily events where the calendar date is irrelevant.
tools.usage:
TimeObject[{h, m, s}]
TimeObject["string"]
TimeObject[date]
TimeObject[{h, m}, TimeZone -> tz]
tools.example:
TimeObject[{14, 30, 0}]
TimeObject["2:30 pm"]
TimeObject[Now]
TimeObject[{9, 0}] < TimeObject[{17, 0}]
DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}, TimeObject[{9, 0}]]

tools.name: TimeZoneConvert
tools.description: Converts a DateObject or TimeObject to a different time zone, preserving the instant in time while changing its representation. Time zones are given as IANA names such as "America/New_York" or as numeric offsets, and daylight saving transitions are handled correctly. It is essential when comparing timestamps from different sources.
tools.example:
TimeZoneConvert[Now, "UTC"]
TimeZoneConvert[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17, 12, 0, 0}, TimeZone -> "UTC"], "Europe/Berlin"]
TimeZoneConvert[Now, -5]
TimeZoneOffset["Asia/Tokyo"]
$TimeZone

tools.name: Now
tools.description: Gives the current date and time as a DateObject in the local time zone, re-evaluated each time it is used. Today gives the current date with day granularity, and Tomorrow and Yesterday are also available. Wrapped in Dynamic with Refresh it produces a live clock.
tools.example:
Now
Today
DateString[Now]
Now - DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}]
Dynamic[Refresh[Now, UpdateInterval -> 1]]
tools.notes: Now is not a constant: each evaluation gives a new value, so assign it to a variable when several computations must use the same instant.

tools.name: $TimeZone
tools.description: The default time zone used when a date is created or displayed without an explicit zone, expressed as an offset from UTC. $TimeZoneEntity gives the corresponding named zone entity and $SystemTimeZone the zone reported by the operating system. Setting $TimeZone in a Block is the clean way to run a computation in another zone.
tools.example:
$TimeZone
$TimeZoneEntity
Block[{$TimeZone = "UTC"}, DateString[Now]]
$SystemTimeZone

tools.name: Entity
tools.description: Represents a real-world object in the Wolfram Knowledgebase, such as a country, chemical, city, planet, species or company, written Entity["type", "name"]. Entities carry thousands of curated properties that can be queried with EntityValue or the shorthand entity["property"]. They evaluate to computable values including quantities with units and geographic positions.
tools.example:
Entity["Country", "France"]
Entity["Country", "France"]["Population"]
Entity["ChemicalElement", "Carbon"]["AtomicMass"]
Entity["City", {"Boston", "Massachusetts", "UnitedStates"}]["Position"]
Entity["Planet", "Mars"]["Mass"]
tools.notes: Knowledgebase access requires an internet connection and a Wolfram account. Use Interpreter["Country"] or free-form input to turn user text into the right entity.

tools.name: EntityValue
tools.description: Retrieves property values for one or many entities in a single call, which is far more efficient than querying them one at a time. Passing lists of entities and properties returns a matrix of values, and the "Dataset" or "PropertyAssociation" forms shape the result. It is the workhorse for pulling curated data into an analysis.
tools.usage:
EntityValue[entity, property]
EntityValue[{e1, e2}, {p1, p2}]
EntityValue[class, props, "Dataset"]
EntityValue["type", "Properties"]
tools.example:
EntityValue[Entity["Country", "France"], "Population"]
EntityValue[{Entity["Country", "France"], Entity["Country", "Spain"]}, {"Population", "Area"}]
EntityValue["Country", "Properties"] // Short
EntityValue[EntityClass["Country", "G7"], {"Name", "GDP"}, "Dataset"]
tools.notes: Batch your queries: one EntityValue call over a list of entities is dramatically faster than mapping over them individually.

tools.name: EntityClass
tools.description: Represents a class of entities, either a named predefined class or one defined by property criteria. EntityClass["Country", "Population" -> TakeLargest[10]] selects the ten most populous countries without enumerating them first. Classes can be passed anywhere an entity list is expected and are resolved lazily by the server.
tools.example:
EntityClass["Country", "Europe"]
EntityClass["Country", "Population" -> TakeLargest[5]]
EntityClass["ChemicalElement", "MeltingPoint" -> GreaterThan[Quantity[2000, "Kelvins"]]]
EntityList[EntityClass["Country", "G7"]]

tools.name: EntityList
tools.description: Expands an entity class or entity type into the explicit list of its member entities. It is how you turn a lazily defined class into concrete entities for iteration. For large types the result can be very long, so combine with an EntityClass filter first.
tools.example:
EntityList[EntityClass["Country", "G7"]]
Length[EntityList["ChemicalElement"]]
EntityList[EntityClass["Country", "Population" -> TakeLargest[3]]]
EntityValue[EntityList[cls], "Name"]

tools.name: EntityProperties
tools.description: Lists the properties available for an entity type or for a specific entity, returned as EntityProperty objects that can be used in EntityValue. It is the discovery tool for the knowledgebase, answering what data exists for a given kind of thing. EntityPropertyClass groups related properties together.
tools.example:
EntityProperties["ChemicalElement"] // Short
Length[EntityProperties["Country"]]
EntityProperty["Country", "Population"]
EntityValue[Entity["Country", "Japan"], EntityProperty["Country", "LifeExpectancy"]]

tools.name: WolframAlpha
tools.description: Sends a natural language query to Wolfram|Alpha and returns the results, either as formatted pods or as computable Wolfram Language expressions. The "Result" element gives the primary answer as an expression, "WolframResult" gives the underlying computation, and "PodPlaintext" gives text. It is the bridge from free-form questions to computable answers.
tools.example:
WolframAlpha["distance from earth to mars", "Result"]
WolframAlpha["population of France", "Result"]
WolframAlpha["integrate x^2 sin x", "WolframResult"]
WolframAlpha["weather in Boston", {{"WeatherCharts:WeatherData", 1}, "Plaintext"}]
tools.notes: Requires an internet connection and consumes Wolfram|Alpha API credits. For structured, repeatable queries the Entity framework is faster and more reliable.

tools.name: Interpreter
tools.description: Parses a string into a typed Wolfram Language value according to a named interpreter type such as "Number", "Date", "Quantity", "City", "Color", "Integer" or a restricted form like Restricted["Integer", 1, 10]. It returns a Failure object when the input cannot be interpreted, which makes it the right tool for validating user input. It is also the mechanism behind APIFunction and FormFunction parameter types.
tools.example:
Interpreter["Number"]["3.14"]
Interpreter["Date"]["next friday"]
Interpreter["Quantity"]["3 miles per hour"]
Interpreter["Country"]["deutschland"]
Interpreter[Restricted["Integer", 1, 10]]["42"]
tools.notes: Simple types such as "Number" and "Integer" work offline; semantic types such as "City" or "Species" require a connection to the Wolfram Knowledgebase.

tools.name: SemanticImport
tools.description: Imports a tabular data file and automatically infers the type of each column, turning text into dates, quantities with units, entities and numbers. The result is a Dataset ready for analysis, with much less cleanup than plain Import. Explicit column type specifications override the automatic inference where it guesses wrong.
tools.example:
SemanticImport["measurements.csv"]
SemanticImport["data.csv", {"Date", "Number", "Quantity"}]
SemanticImportString["date,temp\n2024-05-17,21 C"]
SemanticImport["cities.csv", {"City", "Number"}]
tools.notes: Semantic interpretation of entity columns requires a connection; for purely numeric data plain Import with HeaderLines is faster.

tools.name: GeoPosition
tools.description: Represents a geographic position given as {latitude, longitude} in degrees, optionally with an elevation and a datum. It is the standard coordinate object accepted by all the geographic functions and returned by entity "Position" properties. GeoPositionXYZ, GeoGridPosition and other forms cover alternative coordinate systems.
tools.usage:
GeoPosition[{lat, lon}]
GeoPosition[{lat, lon, elev}]
GeoPosition[{{lat1, lon1}, {lat2, lon2}}]
tools.example:
GeoPosition[{42.36, -71.06}]
Entity["City", {"Paris", "IleDeFrance", "France"}]["Position"]
GeoPosition[{{42.36, -71.06}, {48.85, 2.35}}]
$GeoLocation

tools.name: GeoDistance
tools.description: Computes the distance between two geographic positions or entities along the surface of the Earth, returning a Quantity with length units. The DistanceFunction option selects the geodesic model, with an accurate ellipsoidal geodesic used by default. It accepts city and country entities directly as well as explicit coordinates.
tools.usage:
GeoDistance[loc1, loc2]
GeoDistance[loc1, loc2, DistanceFunction -> f]
GeoDistanceList[locs]
tools.example:
GeoDistance[GeoPosition[{42.36, -71.06}], GeoPosition[{48.85, 2.35}]]
GeoDistance[Entity["City", {"Boston", "Massachusetts", "UnitedStates"}], Entity["City", {"Paris", "IleDeFrance", "France"}]]
UnitConvert[GeoDistance[a, b], "Kilometers"]
GeoDistance[here, there, DistanceFunction -> "Boundary"]

tools.name: GeoNearest
tools.description: Finds the nearest geographic entities of a given type to a location, such as the closest cities, airports, volcanoes or ocean features. A count or a maximum distance limits the results. It is a curated-data spatial query rather than a pure geometry computation.
tools.usage:
GeoNearest["type", location]
GeoNearest["type", location, n]
GeoNearest["type", location, {n, maxdist}]
tools.example:
GeoNearest["City", GeoPosition[{42.36, -71.06}], 5]
GeoNearest["Airport", Entity["City", {"Boston", "Massachusetts", "UnitedStates"}], 3]
GeoNearest["Volcano", GeoPosition[{19.4, -155.3}], {5, Quantity[100, "Kilometers"]}]

tools.name: TextString
tools.description: Converts any expression to a human-readable plain string, formatting dates, quantities, entities and numbers the way a person would write them. It differs from ToString, which produces a programmatic representation. Use it when building messages, labels and report text from computable objects.
tools.example:
TextString[Quantity[3, "Meters"]]
TextString[DateObject[{2024, 5, 17}]]
TextString[Entity["Country", "France"]]
TextString[1/3]
"Total: " <> TextString[Quantity[12.5, "Kilograms"]]

tools.name: TimeSeries
tools.description: Represents a time-indexed sequence of values as a single object supporting resampling, arithmetic, interpolation, windowing and plotting. It accepts date-value pairs or values with an explicit date list, and handles irregular sampling, missing data and time zones. TimeSeriesResample, TimeSeriesWindow, TimeSeriesShift and MovingAverage operate on it directly.
tools.usage:
TimeSeries[{{t1, v1}, {t2, v2}, ...}]
TimeSeries[values, {dates}]
TimeSeriesResample[ts, spec]
TimeSeriesWindow[ts, {start, end}]
tools.example:
ts = TimeSeries[{{DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}], 10}, {DateObject[{2024, 1, 2}], 12}}];
ts["Values"]
ts[DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}]]
TimeSeriesResample[ts, Quantity[1, "Hours"]]
DateListPlot[ts]
tools.notes: EventSeries is the variant for discrete events that should not be interpolated between samples.
